description:
NVIDIA's RTX 3090 Ti GPU launched today, but supply is extremely low due to shutdowns in Shenzhen. The EVGA RTX 3090 Ti is one of the few cards out in the first wave.
Sponsor: Cablemod PCIe Gen. 4 Riser on Amazon: https://geni.us/Yf6qWRs

Watch the tear-down here! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eTFHsRQ-DKM

In this review, we're looking at the RTX 3090 Ti FTW3 that EVGA sent over. The card gets benchmarks for power, thermals, and gaming performance vs. the RTX 3090 non-Ti, RTX 3080, RX 6900 XT, and a few more. We also spent some time overclocking the card. Overall, as it's an ultra high-end enthusiast card, we'll probably spend more time with this under liquid nitrogen once we can get an unlocked VBIOS!

We got this card only 2 full days before launch, so we crammed as many tests in as we could (with a particular focus on thermals and power, given the 450W TDP of the stock 3090 Ti). This was what we could pull together in those two days. We have more we want to do, and that's true basically in every review, but this will help people considering an early purchase of the 3090 Ti.

comments.text:
​ @kingplunger1  TLDR: Fair enough. 

I don't think it applies much to crypto power usage since for those kinds of use cases which scale horizontally, it doesn't really matter what an individual GPU uses. And of course the power used by peoples' single GPUs during gaming is a minuscule portion of the world's total power consumption for computation, let alone the grand total. 

But minuscule or not, it is a nonzero difference and there is an argument to be made for GPU manufacturers artificially limiting their offerings to be more environmentally responsible. I certainly wouldn't argue against that kind of stance. 

Though this seems more like the domain of regulation. Unfortunately I don't think we can rely on companies choosing to limit their own competitiveness. Not with their present incentive alignment.

There's also the fact that these kinds of sensible arguments haven't really been a significant part of the backlash I've come across. But it's certainly possible that what I happened to see wasn't representative. So I can't discount the possibility that all the juvenile nonsense I saw was a loud minority and reasonable concerns such as yours are more common.

I won't buy Nvidia until they start caring about making their GPU's available for everyone.  My last Nvidia purchase was a 2080 Super, and quite frankly I'm thankful that I don't have to use Nvidia gimmicks like DLSS to get the performance I want on everything I've purchased since.  If money is power, use your power to stop companies like this.  That is all.

comments.text:
Surprised you didn't mention the heat. A lot of people don't realize that almost all of that power consumption will be converted into heat and dumped into your room. 
It's basically like buying a 500w space heater. I have a 3080 and it is already way too hot, I routinely undervolt and underpower it just to keep my room manageable. It's actually kind of nice in the winter, but it's terrible in the summer.

@Dennzer1  You seem to be missing the point entirely. The arbitrary AMD numbers you mention are irrelevant. It's extremely obvious that GPUs become more efficient with each generation. The problem is that each generation is now requiring much more more power. Such as in this video, showing the 3090 ti pushing 500 watts, nearly the same as a small space heater. Not to mention the leaks on 4000 series cards requiring even more power, which will surely lead to many users buying much higher rated power supplies. What good is efficiency if you keep increasing the total power draw?

Also there are big inefficiencies with recent generation cards, such as the stock clocks on 3000 series cards. Essentially selling out of the box with very poor overclocks. The proof is in the fact that you can undervolt to increase efficiency. For example I undervolted my 3080 to save over 100 watts at the cost of less than 2% performance. Seems like these cards don't have great power consumption after all.

So yes, again OP's comment is completely true. We are irrefutably seeing higher prices for many reasons, higher power consumption each generation and questionable marketing. Marketing such as selling 3090s as gaming cards (similar cards were previously sold without gaming branding), when they're more tailored to workstations.

I'm not sure why you're so upset by people's opinions, but you should know these are obvious facts. It's a little ironic that you're attempting to be patronizing when you're the one who can't understand these basic principles.

Can you please do some testing on these top end cards when driving a VR headset like the HP Reverb G2 that needs 19 million pixels rendered at 90fps? That's 3172x3100 pixels actually rendered per eye to account for the lens distortion, which is way above what the display stats would indicate.

Sure 8K gaming might not be important at this point. However VR is a very real use case where pixel density to remove the screen door effect has a large impact on the immersion and a stable framerate can have a large impact on motion sickness.

Right now with a FE RTX3090 I can have the games look jaw droppingly beautiful, or I can have them run at a stable framerate. I can't have both.

This will be even more important when Nvidia and AMD raise the bar again with the upcoming generation. Information on how well they handle the high pixel count VR headsets could be some really compelling reason to buy one of these otherwise more business focused cards. Part of the reason I have a 3090 is due to an utter lack of information on how well it vs the 3080 would cope with VR. Even on the day of purchase I was still unsure of my choice and went with which was more likely to stay in stock for a few minutes while I completed my checkout!

@luckyowl10  Nahh, ya'd just trip the breaker. 14 gauge wire (what's in most all modern houses, at least in the US) is capable of carrying over 20 amps safely. That's well over 2000w without burning stuff down.

Circuit breakers generally trip at 14-20 amps, though, and anything over something like 15 amps (maybe 20? It's still 'safe' at 20, after all) is supposed to go up to 12 guage. The margin is there for connection issues and faults to happen without immediately starting a fire: The circuit breaker takes time to trip, so if it tripped AT the actual limit of the wire, it'd probably be too late in particularly faulty conditions.
